slides: Psychometric thinking. We're starting a run of the most important lessons in quantitative reasoning.

slides.say: In these lessons, we'll understand what stands behind the questions on the exam.
That understanding will help you approach the questions in the right way, and in an easier way.
So what is the goal of the psychometric exam? To predict success in academic studies.
It's a sorting exam, so it has to rank the candidates. How does it do that? The questions on the exam are special questions.
What does that mean? Usually, when we solve a question, we use a way we know from school. We plug into a formula, we build an equation, and so on.
at: we use a way we know from school

slides.say: On the exam, in a large part of the questions, there's also a shortcut. Some creative thinking that gets us to the answer faster and more easily.

slides: That's psychometric thinking, and that's what the exam tests. It looks for the students who think this way, and it gives them an advantage.

slides.say: Let's see what that looks like on a small example. Twenty-five times four, times thirty-seven, divided by thirty-seven. The calculating way multiplies everything first, and then divides by thirty-seven. That's long, and it's easy to slip.

The thinking way looks at the numbers first. Times thirty-seven, and then divided by thirty-seven, cancel each other, because dividing undoes the multiplying. So we're left with twenty-five times four, which is a hundred.

One more. Nine hundred ninety-nine, plus nine hundred ninety-nine, plus nine hundred ninety-nine. Instead of adding column by column, think of a thousand. Each one is a thousand minus one. So three of them are three thousand minus three, which is two thousand nine hundred ninety-seven.

Each one is a thousand minus one

slides.say: Why does this work? We didn't skip any math. We looked at the numbers before we started, and we chose an easier way to the same result. So when do we do it? On every question. Before you calculate, take a few seconds to look at the numbers and at the answers. If the calculation looks long, that's a sign there's a shorter way.
